tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Interpret causal convolution by connecting one-sided support and overlap bounds to the LTI output rule that only past input values weighted by the impulse response contribute at time t.

image_slots.image_description: A clean $\tau$-axis schematic for a fixed output time t. Mark t on the $\tau$-axis. Shade the region $\tau \le t and label it present and past input values$. Leave the region $\tau > t unshaded and label it future input values excluded by causality$. Show a generic $x(\tau)$ curve or sample marks over the past region. Show $h(t - \tau)$ as a one-sided weighting function that is nonzero only on the shaded side and zero for $\tau > t$. Do not include numerical signal values or decorative elements.

blocks.text: In causal convolution, the object to watch is the shifted impulse response $h(t - \tau)$. The output time t is fixed, and $\tau$ is the variable that scans through input time values.

A causal impulse response is zero before its input time. For the base case, you can think of a causal exponential such as $h(s)=e$^{-as}$u(s)$ with $a>0$. The important point is the support rule: $h(s)$ is zero when $s<0$.
Now apply that rule to the shifted argument $s=t-\tau$. The shifted response $h(t - \tau)$ can be nonzero only when t - $\tau$ is not negative.

The inequality $\tau \le t$ is the causal cutoff. Values $x(\tau)$ with $\tau \le t$ are present or past input values relative to the output time t. Values with $\tau > t$ are future input values, so a causal LTI system cannot use them to form $y(t)$.

This causal form is only the first support restriction. If $x(\tau)$ is zero on part of the past region, those values still do not contribute. The actual contribution comes from the overlap where $x(\tau)$ and $h(t - \tau)$ are both nonzero.

The interpretation to carry forward is this: causal convolution accumulates weighted past input. At time $t$, each allowed input value $x(\tau)$ is multiplied by the shifted impulse-response weight $h(t - \tau)$, and the integral adds those weighted contributions.

sections.section_title: Identifying Past Input Values at a Fixed Output Time

example_content.example_prompt: For a causal LTI system, identify which input values $x(\tau)$ can contribute to $y(3)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the system is causal. For a causal impulse response, $h(t - \tau)$ can be nonzero only when the input time $\tau$ is not after the output time $t$.

explanation_blocks.latex: h(t-\tau)\text{ can be nonzero only when }\tau\le t

explanation_blocks.text: Here the output time is $t=3$, so substitute $3$ for $t$ in the causal condition.
So the possible contributing input values are $x(\tau)$ with $\tau \le 3$. This includes the present input value at $\tau=3$ and all earlier input times.
Input values with $\tau > 3$ are future values relative to $y(3)$, so they cannot contribute in a causal LTI system.

sections.section_title: Reading Causal Overlap Bounds from One-Sided Supports

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(\tau)$ nonzero on $0 \le \tau \le 4$ and causal $h(t - \tau)$, determine the overlap bounds when $0 \le t \le 4$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that there are now two support restrictions. The active overlap is the set of $\tau$-values where both $x(\tau)$ and $h(t - \tau)$ can be nonzero.
The input support gives the first restriction.
Because $h(t - \tau)$ is causal, the shifted impulse response can be nonzero only for present and past input times.
Now use the given time region, $0 \le t \le 4$. In this region, t lies inside the input support, so the upper overlap limit comes from the causal cutoff $\tau \le t$, not from the endpoint $\tau=4$.
Therefore, the overlap bounds are $0 \le \tau \le t$. These are the input values inside the one-sided input support that are also visible to the causal impulse response at time t.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Shifted Impulse Response as a Weighting Function

example_content.example_prompt: For $h(t) = e^{-2t}u(t)$, interpret $h(5 - \tau)$ as a weighting function on $x(\tau)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the shifted impulse-response factor in the product $x(\tau)h(5 - \tau)$. This factor is the weight applied to each input value $x(\tau)$ when the output time is $t=5$.
Substitute $5 - \tau$ into the impulse response expression.
The unit step decides where this weight can be nonzero. Since $u(5 - \tau)$ is on when $5 - \tau \ge 0$, only $\tau$-values with $\tau \le 5$ can receive a nonzero weight.
So the shifted impulse response acts like this weighting function over input time.
For each allowed past input value, $x(\tau)$ is multiplied by $e^{-2(5 - \tau)}$. Inputs closer to $\tau=5$ receive a larger weight, while farther-past inputs receive a smaller exponential weight.
Values with $\tau > 5$ are future values relative to $y(5)$, so $h(5 - \tau)=0$ there and those input values receive weight zero.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Zero Output from No Past Overlap

example_content.example_prompt: If $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only for $2 \le \tau \le 5$ and $h$ is causal, determine whether $y(t)$ is zero for $t < 2$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the time region $t < 2$, which is before the input support begins. Use the same support-intersection test, but look for whether any overlap exists at all.
The input is nonzero only on this $\tau$-interval.
Because $h$ is causal, $h(t - \tau)$ can be nonzero only for input times in the causal past of $t$.
Now apply the region $t < 2$. If $\tau \le t$ and $t < 2$, then $\tau$ is less than $2$, so those past input times are entirely before the nonzero input support starts.
There is no $\tau$-value where both $x(\tau)$ and $h(t - \tau)$ can be nonzero. The product inside the convolution integral is therefore zero for every $\tau$ in this time region.
So the convolution output is zero for $t < 2$. A causal system cannot respond before any nonzero input value has entered its past.

sections.section_title: Explaining Output as Accumulated Weighted Past Input

example_content.example_prompt: Explain what $y(4) = \int_0^4 x(\tau)e^{-2(4 - \tau)}\,d\tau$ means for a causal convolution with input support starting at $\tau = 0$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the expression is already written as a causal convolution value at one fixed output time. The fixed output time is $t=4$.

The integration interval gives the contributing input times. Since the input support starts at $\tau=0$ and the system is causal, $y(4)$ uses input values from $\tau=0$ through the present time $\tau=4$.
The factor multiplying $x(\tau)$ is the shifted impulse-response weight. For each contributing $\tau$-value, $x(\tau)$ is multiplied by $e^{-2(4 - \tau)}$.
The integral then adds all of those weighted input contributions over the overlap interval. It is not just one input value and it is not unweighted area under $x(\tau)$.
So $y(4)$ means the accumulated weighted past input from $\tau=0$ to $\tau=4$. No $\tau > 4$ input values appear, because those values are future values relative to the output time $t=4$.

sections.section_title: Identifying Past Input Values at a Fixed Output Time

prompt_blocks.text: For a causal LTI system, which input values $x(\tau)$ can contribute to $y(5)$?

choice_blocks.text: Input values $x(\tau)$ with $\tau \ge 5$
Input values $x(\tau)$ with $\tau < 5$
Input values $x(\tau)$ with $\tau \le 5$
Input values $x(\tau)$ for all real $\tau$
Only the input value $x(5)$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For a causal impulse response, $h(t-\tau)$ can be nonzero only when $\tau \le t$. At $t=5$, the contributing input values are therefore $x(\tau)$ with $\tau \le 5$, including $\tau=5$.

prompt_blocks.text: For a causal LTI system, which input values $x(\tau)$ can contribute to $y(-2)$?

choice_blocks.text: Input values $x(\tau)$ with $\tau \le -2$
Input values $x(\tau)$ with $\tau \ge -2$
Input values $x(\tau)$ with $\tau < -2$
Input values $x(\tau)$ with $\tau \le 2$
Input values $x(\tau)$ for all real $\tau$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Causality means the output at time $t$ can depend only on the input at that time and earlier times. For $t=-2$, the possible contributors are exactly the input values with $\tau \le -2$.

sections.section_title: Reading Causal Overlap Bounds from One-Sided Supports

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(\tau)$ nonzero on $0 \le \tau \le 6$ and causal $h(t-\tau)$, what are the overlap bounds when $0 \le t \le 6$?

choice_blocks.text: $0 \le \tau \le 6$
$0 \le \tau \le t$
$\tau \le t$
$t \le \tau \le 6$
$0 \le \tau \le 6-t$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The input support gives $0 \le \tau \le 6$, and causality gives $\tau \le t$. Since $0 \le t \le 6$, the causal cutoff $t$ lies inside the input support, so the intersection is $0 \le \tau \le t$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(\tau)$ nonzero on $0 \le \tau \le 8$ and causal $h(t-\tau)$, what are the overlap bounds when $0 \le t \le 5$?

choice_blocks.text: $0 \le \tau \le 8$
$\tau \le t$
$t \le \tau \le 8$
$0 \le \tau \le t$
$t \le \tau \le 0$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The nonzero input support is $0 \le \tau \le 8$. Causality adds the restriction $\tau \le t$. In the region $0 \le t \le 5$, $t$ is still before the endpoint $8$, so the overlap is $0 \le \tau \le t$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Shifted Impulse Response as a Weighting Function

prompt_blocks.text: For $h(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$, which statement correctly interprets $h(4-\tau)$ as a weighting function on $x(\tau)$?

choice_blocks.text: It weights each allowed past input value with $\tau \le 4$ by $e^{-3(4-\tau)}$ and gives zero weight for $\tau>4$.
It applies the weight $e^{-3(4-\tau)}$ only to future input values with $\tau>4$.
It gives every input value $x(\tau)$ the same constant weight $e^{-12}$.
It weights each allowed past input value with $\tau \le 4$ by $e^{3(4-\tau)}$ and gives zero weight for $\tau>4$.
It is nonzero for input values with $\tau \ge 4$ and uses the weight $e^{-3(4-\tau)}$ there.

questions.correct_answer: It weights each allowed past input value with $\tau \le 4$ by $e^{-3(4-\tau)}$ and gives zero weight for $\tau>4$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substituting $4-\tau$ gives $h(4-\tau)=e^{-3(4-\tau)}u(4-\tau)$. The unit step is on when $4-\tau\ge 0$, so only $\tau\le 4$ receives the exponential weight.

prompt_blocks.text: For $h(t)=e^{-4t}u(t)$, which statement correctly interprets $h(2-\tau)$ as a weighting function on $x(\tau)$?

choice_blocks.text: It means the shifted input $x(2-\tau)$ is weighted by $e^{-4\tau}$.
It weights each allowed past input value with $\tau \le 2$ by $e^{-4(2-\tau)}$ and gives zero weight for $\tau>2$.
It applies the weight $e^{-4(2-\tau)}$ to future input values with $\tau>2$ and gives zero weight for $\tau\le 2$.
It gives every input value $x(\tau)$ the same constant weight $e^{-8}$.
It weights each allowed past input value with $\tau \le 2$ by $e^{4(2-\tau)}$ and gives zero weight for $\tau>2$.

questions.correct_answer: It weights each allowed past input value with $\tau \le 2$ by $e^{-4(2-\tau)}$ and gives zero weight for $\tau>2$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shifted response is $h(2-\tau)=e^{-4(2-\tau)}u(2-\tau)$. Since $u(2-\tau)$ is nonzero only when $\tau\le 2$, only those past input values receive the exponential weight.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Zero Output from No Past Overlap

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only for $1 \le \tau \le 4$ and $h$ is causal, which conclusion is correct for $t<1$?

choice_blocks.text: $y(t)=0$ for $t<1$, because the causal past region $\tau\le t$ has no overlap with $1\le \tau\le 4$.
$y(t)$ is nonzero for $t<1$ because a causal system uses past input values.
$y(t)=0$ only for $t<0$; for $0\le t<1$ there is already input overlap.
$y(t)=0$ for $t>4$ because the input support has ended, so $t<1$ is not the zero-output region.
The conclusion cannot be determined unless the support of $h(\tau)$ is given directly.

questions.correct_answer: $y(t)=0$ for $t<1$, because the causal past region $\tau\le t$ has no overlap with $1\le \tau\le 4$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Causality gives the shifted-response condition $\tau\le t$. If $t<1$, then all allowed past input times satisfy $\tau<1$, which is before the nonzero support $1\le \tau\le 4$. There is no overlap, so $y(t)=0$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only for $3 \le \tau \le 8$ and $h$ is causal, which conclusion is correct for $t<3$?

choice_blocks.text: $y(t)$ is nonzero for $t<3$ because causality means the system responds to past inputs.
$y(t)=0$ only for $t<0$; for $0\le t<3$ the delayed input support has already overlapped.
$y(t)=0$ for $t<3$, because $\tau\le t$ lies entirely before the support $3\le \tau\le 8$.
$y(t)=0$ for $t>8$, so the no-overlap conclusion applies after the input support ends rather than before it begins.
The conclusion cannot be determined from support rules because the formula for $h(t-\tau)$ is not specified.

questions.correct_answer: $y(t)=0$ for $t<3$, because $\tau\le t$ lies entirely before the support $3\le \tau\le 8$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For a causal impulse response, $h(t-\tau)$ can be nonzero only when $\tau\le t$. When $t<3$, those possible input times are all before $\tau=3$, so they do not intersect the support $3\le \tau\le 8$. Therefore the convolution output is zero in this region.

sections.section_title: Explaining Output as Accumulated Weighted Past Input

prompt_blocks.text: Which statement correctly explains $y(6)=\int_0^6 x(\tau)e^{-3(6-\tau)}\,d\tau$ for a causal convolution with input support starting at $\tau=0$?

choice_blocks.text: It accumulates input values from $\tau=0$ to $\tau=6$, with each $x(\tau)$ weighted by $e^{-3(6-\tau)}$.
It is the unweighted area under $x(\tau)$ from $\tau=0$ to $\tau=6$.
It includes future input values with $\tau>6$ because those values come after the output time.
It describes only the impulse response over $0\le \tau\le 6$, not the input values.
It says only the single input value $x(6)$ contributes to the output.

questions.correct_answer: It accumulates input values from $\tau=0$ to $\tau=6$, with each $x(\tau)$ weighted by $e^{-3(6-\tau)}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The bounds $0\le \tau\le 6$ give the contributing past input times. The factor $e^{-3(6-\tau)}$ is the shifted impulse-response weight applied to each $x(\tau)$ before the integral adds the contributions.

prompt_blocks.text: Which statement correctly explains $y(5)=\int_1^5 x(\tau)e^{-2(5-\tau)}\,d\tau$ for a causal convolution with input support starting at $\tau=1$?

choice_blocks.text: It is the unweighted area under $x(\tau)$ from $\tau=1$ to $\tau=5$.
It includes input values after $t=5$ because future values are included in the convolution integral.
It accumulates input values from $\tau=1$ to $\tau=5$, with each $x(\tau)$ weighted by $e^{-2(5-\tau)}$.
It is a frequency-domain description of how the system scales sinusoidal inputs.
It says only the impulse response value $e^{-2(5-\tau)}$ matters; the input $x(\tau)$ does not affect the output.

questions.correct_answer: It accumulates input values from $\tau=1$ to $\tau=5$, with each $x(\tau)$ weighted by $e^{-2(5-\tau)}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The integral uses input times $1\le \tau\le 5$, ending at the output time $t=5$. Each contributing input value $x(\tau)$ is multiplied by the shifted impulse-response weight $e^{-2(5-\tau)}$, then those weighted contributions are accumulated.
